title: Snakebite: what to do
asks: snake bit me what do i do
bitten by a rattlesnake what now
buddy got bit by a snake on the ankle
how to treat a snake bite in the field

do i keep a snake bite above or below the heart

answer: Get medical help immediately. Anyone bitten by a snake, venomous or not, should seek medical attention right away.
Stay calm. Keep the bitten person as still as possible: movement and exertion can speed the spread of venom.
Do not try to catch, kill or identify the snake. It is dangerous, wastes time and is not needed for treatment.

Never touch a snake's head, even if the snake is dead or its head is cut off: it can still bite and inject venom. WHO: if it can be done from a distance without risk, take a picture of the snake to send with the patient.
Remove rings, jewelry and tight clothing from the bitten area, because it may swell.
Keep the bitten limb slightly below the level of the heart, if possible.
Gently wash the bite with mild soap and water.
Cover the bite with a sterile bandage or dressing: snug, but not too tight.
Loosely immobilize the bitten limb to reduce movement, without constricting it.
With a marker, circle the bite and write the time of the bite on the skin. Mark the edge of the pain and the edge of the swelling, and note the time.
Antivenom is the main treatment. If none is on hand, get the person to a medical facility that has antivenom as fast as safely possible, even if they have to walk.
Watch their breathing and heart rate, keep the airway open (especially if the bite is near the face or neck), and be prepared to give CPR if needed.
During evacuation, watch for signs of an allergic reaction, treat for shock and keep the person warm.
In the United States, a medical toxicologist can be reached through a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222.
warnings: Do not use a tourniquet or ice: they are not effective and can cause additional harm.

If a tourniquet or tight band is already on, do not take it off in the field: removing it can cause sudden collapse. The Joint Trauma System guideline says to leave it until medical staff are ready to treat and resuscitate the person.
Do not cut the bite open or try to suck out the venom.

Sources differ on tight bands and bandages. The Joint Trauma System snakebite guideline says do NOT apply constricting bandages: they may worsen tissue injury. The Army survival manual says to use a constricting band between the wound and the heart. WHO says a firm, broad pressure bandage may be used: it is recommended where local snakes cause nerve damage, paralysis or severe illness, or where transport will be long, and NOT recommended where the venom mainly damages tissue near the bite without body-wide symptoms.

quotes.text: Venomous snakes DO NOT always inject venom when they bite or strike a person. However, all snakes may carry tetanus (lockjaw); anyone bitten by a snake, whether venomous or nonvenomous, should immediately seek medical attention.

Stay calm and call for medical assistance immediately. Provide medical personnel with information about the snake, if possible, but do not attempt to capture or kill the snake as it may increase the risk of further bites.
Keep the bitten Service member as still and calm as possible. Restrict movement and avoid unnecessary exertion, as it can accelerate the spread of venom in the bloodstream.
Don’t try to ID the snake. You don’t need to know the snake’s species to treat the patient. Trying to catch or kill the snake is dangerous and wastes time. Focus on the patient’s symptoms.
In the event you are bitten, do not attempt to identify and or kill the snake. Freshly killed snakes can continue to bite due to reflexive action. Snake identification is not critical.
DO NOT take risks to obtain photos! Never touch the head with your hands - even a decapitated snake head can bite and inject venom >24 hours after the bite.
If snake bite is suspected, immobilize the limb. [See SKILLS] Take a picture of the snake if possible from a distance and send with patient. Do not risk additional bites to catch/kill snake.
Remove any constricting items, such as jewelry or tight clothing, from the affected area, as swelling may occur.
Position the affected limb slightly below the level of the heart, if possible. This can help slow the spread of venom.
When treating a snakebite, be sure to keep the extremity lower than the heart.
Cleanse the wound gently with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Do not apply ice or use a TQ, as they are not effective and can cause additional harm.
Apply a sterile bandage or dress over the bite, ensuring it is snug but not too tight. This can help immobilize the area and reduce the spread of venom.

If and when conditions allow, minimize patient activity, and loosely immobilize the bitten limb to reduce movement without constricting tissues. a. If antivenom isn’t available, get the patient to a facility with antivenom as fast as safely possible, even if they have to walk.
On bitten limb in Sharpie: Circle bite wound, record time when bite occurred
Mark the edge of pain (dashed line) and swelling (solid line) with a marker and note the time.

Antivenom is the gold standard of care for symptomatic snake envenomations. Early treatment is the best strategy to prevent death, amputation, or other serious disability. Management of snake envenomations when antivenom is not available should be directed at getting the patient to the antivenom (or vice versa) as quickly as possible to prevent irreversible damage to organs and tissues.
Encourage the person to remain calm and still, while waiting for medical help to arrive. Monitor their vital signs, such as breathing and heart rate, and be prepared to administer CPR if necessary.
Maintain an airway (especially if bitten near the face or neck) and be prepared to administer mouth-to-mouth resuscitation or cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

If accompanying the casualty on CASEVAC to an MTF, observe the casualty carefully for signs and symptoms of an allergic reaction. Continue to monitor the airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs (for first aid purposes; pulse, and respiration), and distal pulse of the bitten extremity, treating for shock, and conserving body heat.
Consult a Medical Toxicologist as soon as possible. Within the United States, a Medical Toxicologist can be reached via a Poison Control Center by calling 800-222-1222.
If a tourniquet is already in place, see Tourniquet Algorithm. Do not remove it until you are ready to treat and resuscitate the patient as a rapid decompensation can occur.
Tourniquets and constricting bands may worsen snakebite outcomes and must be removed according to the Tourniquet Algorithm.
DO NOT attempt to cut open the bite or suck out the venom. If the venom should seep through any damaged or lacerated tissues in your mouth, you could immediately lose consciousness or even die.
DO NOT apply constricting bandages or tourniquets as these may worsen local tissue injury and increase the risk of permanent disability.
Use a constricting band between the wound and the heart.

You may choose to use a broad pressure bandage and wrap upwards from the lower portion of the bite. The bandage should be firm, but should not cut off pulses in the limb. Extend the bandage as high up the limb as possible. –– This is recommended if the snakes in your area produce a toxin that damages the nerves, causes paralysis, causes the person to become very ill or if there will be prolonged transport time. –– This is NOT recommended if the snakes in your area produce toxins that primarily cause tissue damage near the wound and do not cause body-wide symptoms.

conflict: (1) Constricting bands and pressure bandages: JTS Snakebite CPG (2026) says 'DO NOT apply constricting bandages or tourniquets' and ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says no tourniquet, bandage 'snug but not too tight'; Army ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says 'Use a constricting band between the wound and the heart'; WHO BEC (2018) allows a broad pressure bandage, recommended only where local snakes cause nerve damage or paralysis, severe illness, or transport is prolonged, and NOT recommended where venom mainly causes tissue damage near the wound. The card shows all three positions in one warning; the owner must choose. (2) Identifying the snake: ATP 3-50.21 says to determine first whether the snake was venomous, from the bite marks; JTS says 'Don't rely on fang marks' and not to try to identify the snake; WHO BEC says to take a picture of the snake from a distance if possible and ATP 4-02.11 says to give medical personnel information about the snake if possible. The card follows JTS and ATP 4-02.11 and shows the WHO picture advice, attributed. (3) Movement: WHO BEC says 'Keep the person still and lying down'; JTS says minimize activity but get to antivenom 'even if they have to walk'. (4) Limb position: the card's 'slightly below the heart' is field guidance (ATP 4-02.11, ATP 3-50.21, JTS during transport); JTS says to elevate the limb once the patient is at a facility with antivenom. (5) A tourniquet or band that is already on: JTS says not to remove it until ready to treat and resuscitate, and that such bands 'must be removed according to the Tourniquet Algorithm'; that algorithm is a figure with no extractable text, so the kit gives no removal steps and no time limit; ATP 3-50.21 recommends a constricting band. The owner should confirm the 'leave it on' wording for long evacuations. HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) and FEMA P-2064 (2020) were searched: neither covers snakebite treatment.
